candidates.slide_ref: Lecture 02 - Java Basics - Part I.pptx slide 63
candidates.snippet: Java characters use Unicode, a 16-bit encoding scheme established by the Unicode Consortium to support the interchange, processing, and display of written texts in the world's diverse languages. Unicode takes two bytes, preceded by \u, expressed in four hexadecimal numbers that run from '\u0000' to '\uFFFF'. So, Unicode can represent 65535 + 1 characters.
candidates.prima_facie_concern: Conflates Unicode with UTF-16 / Java's `char` type. Unicode itself is not a 16-bit encoding scheme — it defines code points up to U+10FFFF (≈1.1 million), far more than 65,536. Java's `char` is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit and characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane require surrogate pairs. The claim 'Unicode can represent 65535 + 1 characters' has been factually wrong since Unicode 2.0 (1996).

candidates.prima_facie_concern: Uses the integer rounding-mode constant `BigDecimal.ROUND_UP`. These integer rounding-mode constants on `BigDecimal` (`ROUND_UP`, `ROUND_HALF_EVEN`, etc.) have been deprecated since JDK 9 in favor of the `java.math.RoundingMode` enum (e.g., `RoundingMode.UP`). (1) `new Integer(3)` and `new Integer(5)` — the `Integer(int)` constructor has been deprecated since JDK 9; `Integer.valueOf(3)` (or simple boxing) is preferred.
